output.summary: Cavernous malformations are a recognized structural cause of focal epilepsy; susceptibility-weighted imaging is the most sensitive sequence for them and for additional lesions. Resection can be considered for cavernoma-related epilepsy, particularly when seizures persist on medication. Initial monotherapy evidence for focal seizures in adults is strongest for carbamazepine, levetiracetam, phenytoin and zonisamide.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not manage the outside report of a 'possible prior small hemorrhage' as an acute hemorrhage: the hemosiderin rim, mixed-age blood products and absence of edema or restricted diffusion indicate a chronic cavernous malformation.
Do not give thrombolytic or anticoagulant therapy on a misdiagnosis of acute stroke; the events are stereotyped focal seizures from a chronic cavernoma.
Do not perform lumbar puncture; there is no clinical feature of CNS infection or inflammation.
Do not accept a standard brain MRI without susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo sequences as characterization of the lesion.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for a woman of childbearing potential with no interacting medicines (slow lamotrigine titration; mood monitoring on levetiracetam).
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.
Test HLA-B*15:02 before any carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
Refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation of the right mesial temporal cavernous malformation.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, without meningism, encephalopathy or immunosuppression, and with a structural lesion that explains three months of stereotyped focal seizures; CSF has no question to answer.

Ear-fullness auras, oral and manual automatisms and postictal confusion without a syncopal prodrome, a normal ECG and a right temporal EEG focus; cardiac monitoring is not indicated.
Inpatient evaluation without head injury, new deficit or anticoagulation and with MRI available; CT cannot characterize a cavernous malformation and adds radiation.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin (cavernous malformation)

differential.diagnosis: Hemorrhagic low-grade temporal neoplasm (e.g., ganglioglioma with hemorrhage)
differential.key_features: Hemorrhagic low-grade tumors can mimic a cavernoma, but usually show a solid or enhancing component, an incomplete hemosiderin rim or edema; the complete rim, mixed-age blood products, no enhancement and no edema on the epilepsy-protocol MRI make it unlikely. Follow-up imaging or histology settles any residual doubt.

differential.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy secondary to hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis)
differential.key_features: Normal bilateral hippocampal volumes and normal T2/FLAIR signal on epilepsy-protocol MRI; cavernoma is the concordant lesion.

differential.diagnosis: Cavernous malformation presenting as acute hemorrhage (mimicking stroke)
differential.key_features: No acute restricted diffusion, edema or mass effect, a chronic hemosiderin rim and three months of stereotyped focal seizures distinguish a chronic epileptogenic cavernoma from an acute hemorrhage.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (type II) of right temporal lobe
differential.key_features: No cortical thickening, gray-white blurring or transmantle sign on the epilepsy-protocol MRI; the cavernoma accounts for the findings.
Video-EEG captured two habitual events with a right anterior temporal ictal onset; a concordant structural lesion is present.

key_clinical_evidence: Weekly stereotyped episodes of behavioral arrest, oral and manual automatisms, amnesia and postictal confusion over three months are focal impaired-awareness seizures and meet the two-seizure definition of epilepsy.

The outside report of a 'possible prior small hemorrhage' does not indicate an acute event: the complete hemosiderin rim, popcorn mixed signal, SWI blooming far exceeding the lesion and absence of edema or enhancement identify a chronic cavernous malformation, not an acute vascular event.
Susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo sequences are needed to characterize a suspected cavernoma and to look for additional lesions.

Localization rests on the concordance of the right anterior temporal interictal focus and ictal onset with the right mesial temporal cavernoma; the left-hand automatisms and leftward head turning lateralize weakly (unilateral manual automatisms are more often ipsilateral to the onset).

She is left-handed, so language dominance is uncertain until tested; the neuropsychological profile (visual memory and visuospatial weakness, intact verbal memory) points to right-hemisphere dysfunction.
An epileptogenic cavernous malformation is a potentially surgically remediable cause of focal epilepsy.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The outside description of 'possible prior small hemorrhage' corresponds to the hemosiderin-laden cavernous malformation visible on dedicated epilepsy MRI with GRE/SWI. Chronic hemosiderin blooming, popcorn T2 morphology, absence of DWI restriction, and absence of perilesional edema all confirm a chronic epileptogenic cavernoma, not an acute or subacute hemorrhagic event requiring vascular intervention.

red_herrings.intended_effect: An unwary agent may anchor on 'prior hemorrhage' and pursue an acute vascular workup (CT, echo, cardiac monitoring, stroke protocol) rather than recognizing this as a known chronic cavernoma pattern requiring epilepsy-protocol MRI with GRE/SWI for characterization.

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Hayashi is a 38-year-old left-handed East Asian software engineer who presents to the epilepsy monitoring unit for evaluation of recurrent stereotyped spells that have occurred approximately weekly over the past three months. She has no prior history of seizures or neurological illness.

The patient reports that the episodes begin abruptly without clear warning, though on two occasions she noticed a brief sensation of unusual fullness or pressure in her right ear followed by a rising feeling of anxiety immediately before the event. She has no memory of the episodes themselves. Her husband has witnessed two events. He describes her suddenly stopping mid-conversation and staring blankly, then beginning repetitive chewing and swallowing motions. During the most recent episode three days ago, she fumbled with nearby objects with her left hand for approximately 45 to 60 seconds. On one occasion, her head turned slowly to the left. After the episode ended, she appeared confused and disoriented for approximately five minutes before returning to her baseline. She was fatigued for several hours afterward.

The episodes do not involve falls, urinary incontinence, or tongue biting. She denies any preceding headache, visual changes, palpitations, or lightheadedness. She has no history of migraines. There is no history of febrile illness, recent travel, or systemic symptoms. She has not started or changed any medications recently. She is not pregnant.

She was seen two weeks ago by an outside neurologist who ordered a standard MRI brain without epilepsy protocol. The radiologist's report noted a 'small focus of T2 signal and possible prior small hemorrhage in the right temporal lobe' and recommended clinical correlation, but the clinical significance was not further characterized at that visit. The patient was referred for inpatient evaluation at our center.

neurological_exam.additional: No postictal deficits at examination; the most recent episode was three days ago. Husband describes witnessed events as brief behavioral arrest with mouth-chewing and fumbling movements of the left hand, followed by a period of confusion lasting several minutes. Head turning to the left was observed during one episode.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally without dysmetria or intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact and symmetric.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light bilaterally (4 mm to 2.5 mm). Visual fields full to confrontation in all four quadrants bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick in all three trigeminal divisions bilaterally. Facial movements symmetric at rest and with volitional activation. Hearing intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically. Gag reflex present bilaterally. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline, no atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait with symmetric arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody; no paraphasic errors. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Registers 3/3 objects; recalls 3/3 at five minutes without cues. Able to spell WORLD backwards. Serial 7s performed without error. Draws intersecting pentagons accurately. Visuospatial constructional ability intact. No left-right confusion.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone in all four extremities. No spasticity, rigidity, or involuntary movements. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups bilaterally (deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger abductors, iliopsoas, quadriceps, hamstrings, tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius). No pronator drift observed. No tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and joint position sense intact throughout. No extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.
